title: The funeral prayer
hook: a prayer said standing, with no bowing and no prostration, and a duty on the whole community

segments.voice: Yesterday, kafan, the shroud, and your line: everyone in white. Did you catch yourself sizing someone up, and see the person instead? Today, the community stands before the one in white. Day one thousand three hundred forty-one.

After a regular prayer at the mosque, sometimes the imam turns and says a few quiet words, and people who came only for the noon prayer stay standing. A body, wrapped in white, has been placed at the front. Rows form behind it. And then comes a prayer unlike the others of the day. Nobody bows. Nobody goes down to the ground. The whole prayer happens standing up, and it's over in a few minutes. Some in those rows never met the person, and they are praying for them now.
screen: `A BODY AT THE FRONT.` → `ROWS FORM BEHIND IT.` → `NOBODY BOWS. NOBODY KNEELS.`

segments.voice: It's called salat al-janazah, the funeral prayer. Al-Bukhari keeps a report that shows its shape. When the Negus, the king of Abyssinia, died far away, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, announced his death to the people on the very day it happened. He went out with them to the place of prayer, lined them up in rows, and said Allahu akbar four times. That's the frame: standing, in rows, with four takbirs. In common practice, between them come the opening of the Qur'an, blessings on the Prophet, and du'a for the one who has died, though the schools of law differ on some details. Al-Bukhari also reports that Ibn 'Abbas recited al-Fatiha in a funeral prayer and said he did it so people would know it was the sunnah. Why standing only? One reading is simple: the prayer is for someone else. You stand before Allah on another person's behalf, asking mercy for them. The jurists call it fard kifayah, a communal duty. If some of the community do it, the duty is lifted from the rest. If nobody does, the whole community is at fault. The obligation belongs to everyone together. And there's a reward for whoever shows up. In al-Bukhari, the Prophet said, in paraphrase: whoever attends a funeral until the prayer has a qirat, and whoever stays until the burial has two. Someone asked what two qirats were. Like two huge mountains, he said. Showing up, standing, is the gift. The person in white can't ask. The community stands for them.
screen: `FOUR TAKBIRS, STANDING, IN ROWS.` · `FATIHA, BLESSINGS, AND DU'A.` · `A COMMUNAL DUTY.` · `TWO QIRATS, LIKE TWO MOUNTAINS.`

segments.voice: The practice: join a janazah when you can. Settle, and breathe. Stand up, if you're able, feet planted, hands still. Feel what it's like to stand for a while without any other movement. Now think of someone who has died: someone you knew, or a stranger whose name you heard. Stay standing for them, quietly, for a few breaths. If you pray, you can ask mercy for them in your own words. If you'd like, decide that the next time a janazah is announced near you, you'll stay for it. The bell holds the time.
Salat al-janazah. The funeral prayer: said standing, with four takbirs, no bowing, a duty the community carries together. Today's word.

Your line: stand for them. Today, if you hear of a death, near or far, stop for a moment and stand for them, even in your mind. Tomorrow, burial facing the qiblah. Day one thousand three hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Muslims pray salat al-janazah standing in rows behind the body, with four takbirs and no bowing or prostration, usually reciting al-Fatiha, blessings on the Prophet and a du'a for the deceased; the schools differ on some details.

original.note: Arabic: a funeral, or the bier and the body on it.

trapdoor: what you thought: the funeral prayer is a service for the family.
what it means: a standing prayer with four takbirs, asking mercy for the one who died, a duty the whole community carries.
what a scholar hears: the Negus prayed over from afar with four takbirs, Ibn 'Abbas reciting al-Fatiha as sunnah, and fard kifayah.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1245 (the Negus: rows, four takbirs)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1335 (Ibn 'Abbas recited al-Fatiha in the funeral prayer, as sunnah)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1325 (a qirat for the prayer, two for the burial, like two great mountains)

notes: Bukhari 1245, 1325 and 1335 paraphrased; confirm numbers and details.
The order 'Fatiha, blessings on the Prophet, du'a' is given as 'common practice' with a note that schools differ (the Hanafi school does not recite al-Fatiha as such); confirm phrasing.
Fard kifayah is a juristic classification, not stated in the cited hadith; confirm phrasing.
'One reading' of why the prayer is standing only is interpretive; confirm or cut.
Original-language note: جنازة/جِنازة can be voweled janazah or jinazah; confirm.
Editor: hook softened ('unlike every other one' to 'unlike the others'; 'strangers' praying now 'some in those rows').
